nameStory: The Sea Lemon gets its delightful name from its bright yellow color and oval, slightly bumpy shape that resembles a fresh lemon sitting on the ocean floor. When early marine naturalists first encountered these cheerful sea slugs, the resemblance to citrus fruit was so striking that the common name stuck across many languages and cultures.
description: The Sea Lemon is a type of nudibranch, which is a soft-bodied sea slug that breathes through feathery gills on its back. These charming marine creatures are typically bright yellow to pale orange, with a rounded, dome-shaped body that can grow to about 4 inches long. Unlike snails, they have no shell, and their soft, squishy bodies are covered in small bumps called tubercles that give them a textured, warty appearance. Two horn-like tentacles called rhinophores stick up from their head, helping them smell and taste the water around them.

idTips.label: Bright yellow coloration
idTips.description: Vibrant lemon-yellow to pale orange body that stands out against dark rocks and seaweed, sometimes with white or darker yellow spots scattered across the surface

idTips.label: Bumpy texture
idTips.description: Body feels soft and squishy like a wet sponge, covered in small rounded bumps (tubercles) that give it a warty, textured surface rather than smooth skin

idTips.label: Feathery gill cluster
idTips.description: A circular crown of delicate, feathery white or pale yellow gills at the rear end of the back that can retract when touched or disturbed

idTips.label: Horn-like rhinophores
idTips.description: Two club-shaped tentacles on the head that look like tiny antlers, usually darker than the body and able to retract into sheaths when threatened

idTips.label: Oval dome shape
idTips.description: Rounded, dome-like profile when viewed from the side, roughly oval when seen from above, resembling half of a lemon cut lengthwise

habitat: Sea Lemons live in rocky intertidal zones and subtidal areas along New England's coast, typically found under rocks, in tide pools, or crawling on kelp and other seaweeds. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are most commonly spotted during low tide when they're exposed in shallow pools or clinging to the undersides of large rocks. Look for them in depths from the low tide line down to about 100 feet, often in areas where sponges (their favorite food) are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Most active and visible as water temperatures begin to warm, often found moving across rocks and feeding on sponges. This is peak mating season when you might spot pairs or small groups together.
seasonality.summer: Easily found during low tides in tide pools and under rocks. Adults are at their largest size and most colorful, making them easiest to identify during summer explorations.
seasonality.fall: Still active and feeding heavily before winter, but may be found deeper in crevices and under larger rocks as water temperatures begin to cool.
seasonality.winter: Less active and harder to find, often hiding deep in rock crevices or moving to slightly deeper water. They become sluggish in cold water but don't completely disappear.

funFact: Sea Lemons are actually solar-powered recyclers! They eat colorful sponges and can incorporate the sponge's defensive chemicals into their own skin, making them taste terrible to predators while keeping the bright warning colors that say 'don't eat me!'
confusionNotes: Sea Lemons might be confused with other yellow nudibranchs, but most others are much smaller and have different gill arrangements. Remember: if it's bright yellow, lemon-sized, and has a circular crown of feathery gills on its back, you've found a Sea Lemon!
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'Sea Lemon,' these creatures are not related to citrus fruits or plants at all - they're mollusks, more closely related to snails and clams. The 'nudibranch' name means 'naked gills,' referring to their exposed, feathery breathing organs that stick out from their backs unlike the hidden gills of most other mollusks.
compareHints: As the only Archidoris species commonly found in New England waters, Sea Lemons are distinguished from other dorid nudibranchs by their large size, bright yellow coloration, and distinctive bumpy texture. Other yellow nudibranchs in the region are typically much smaller (under an inch), have smoother bodies, or have different gill arrangements that don't form the characteristic circular crown pattern.
